prize_parts.citation: For empirical analyses of how technological change and international trade reshape labour demand, wage inequality and the adjustment of local labour markets.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1, but several parts of the argument are now sharper. The achievement I would credit is one question: why labour demand and the wage structure moved as they did, and who bore the costs of adjustment. Katz and Murphy, and later Autor, Katz and Kearney, established the skill-demand and wage-structure facts. Autor, Dorn and Hanson showed with transparent designs that import competition produced large, slow and place-specific adjustment. Autor is the one person who spans both strands. Katz anchors the older evidence, which has been confirmed over roughly three decades. Hanson anchors the trade-shock evidence. As an economic historian, I find that the long-run wage-structure series and the local adjustment studies support each other. Together they show that structural change is not quick reallocation but a prolonged and uneven process. That is the kind of result that changes how we understand what we know. The reading of the discussion also supports the choice. The chair summary shows that Autor and Hanson are common to all seven B009 proposals, and that no member rejects either trio. The open choice is Katz or Dorn, and the evidence I have been given does not favour one by merit alone. It depends on whether the committee defines the discovery broadly or narrowly. I hold the broad definition because it is the more coherent one. A citation limited to the China shock rests on the least settled part of the evidence base, while the wage-structure work gives the shock results their interpretive frame. I would word the citation around empirical analysis only, so that it does not claim the task-based theory.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution. The cap excludes David Dorn, a full co-author of the central China-shock papers, and the cost is real. The task framework also has originators who are not on the ballot (Levy and Murnane, and Acemoglu and Restrepo on theory). Some members, including Boppart and Friberg, see two discoveries bundled into one citation, and the broad trio makes that criticism sharper. Katz's long-run skill-premium work is also linked to Goldin's research, as Dreber Almenberg notes, so the marginal credit after the 2023 prize is harder to defend than for the trade-shock strand. The persistence, magnitude and external validity of the shift-share estimates remain debated, as members on all sides concede. B014 has a more compact core, and a committee that judges B009 to be two discoveries could reasonably prefer it.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg now proposes Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and argues that Katz's best-known work on education and technology is closely tied to Goldin's research. This makes his marginal credit harder to defend after the 2023 prize and moves the prize toward a comparison with a prior award.
responses.response: I take this as the strongest argument against keeping Katz, and it is the point I tested most carefully. Katz and Goldin do have a joint line on education and technology, so the thematic overlap is real. My reading is that the 2023 citation was about women's labour-market outcomes over two centuries, and the credit I would give Katz is different: the skill-demand and wage-structure evidence from the early 1990s onward, and the Autor-Katz-Kearney work on polarisation. I therefore see overlap in subject, not duplicate recognition. I accept that the citation must state this explicitly. If the committee reads the overlap differently from me, the cost falls on Katz and not on the Autor-Hanson core, and I would then prefer your trio to a vaguer citation. That is the condition under which I would move.

responses.point: Teorell prefers Autor, Hanson and Dorn so that the citation matches a single identifiable discovery, the China shock. He would accept the Katz version if the committee decides the broader framing is the discovery, as long as it says plainly that a China-shock co-author is being left out.
responses.response: We agree on the structure of the decision, and I would answer the chair's question directly. If the committee defines the discovery narrowly as the trade-shock evidence, I would prefer your trio, and I would not oppose it. If it defines the discovery as the combined account of technology, trade and wage inequality, Katz belongs in it. I hold the broader view with moderate confidence because of one asymmetry. The trade-shock strand is the one with the most debate over persistence and external validity. The wage-structure strand is older and better confirmed, so a prize that rests only on the first strand carries the most evidentiary risk. I also accept your point that the citation should state plainly that the choice follows the three-name cap and does not diminish Dorn's role.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B014 and treats B009 as two strands, technology and trade, whose credit is hard to put into one citation. He adds that the overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes weakens the technology strand's marginal novelty and that the three-name cap forces an uncomfortable exclusion of Dorn.
responses.response: The bundling worry is fair and it is the main reason I list B014 as my first alternative. I resolve it differently. I regard the two strands as one explanatory question about labour demand, with Autor as the bridge between them, and not as separate prizes. The test I would apply is whether a single citation sentence can name the shared object without claiming either strand's theory. I think this one can: labour demand, wage inequality and local adjustment under technology and trade. If the committee decides that test fails, I would move toward B014, because its core is a single framework. I would not decide by comparing the number of members who prefer each, since that count is not scientific merit.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B014 and says a prize for B009 as a whole needs Autor, Hanson and Katz. He notes that Dorn's omission is then a real cost, and that the Dorn swap would make the prize mainly about the China shock. He also sees the priority issues in B014 as smaller than the Dorn-or-Katz and bundling questions.
responses.response: I agree with your first point, and I think it supports the Katz trio. If the broad discovery is the one being credited, Katz is the right third name, and the omission of Dorn then has to be acknowledged openly. On the comparison, I would weigh the two sets of issues differently. The priority claims in B014 (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum, Hopenhayn) and the Arkolakis et al. result are questions about what the framework discovered, and a citation can only narrow them. The Dorn-or-Katz choice is a question about who is named within an agreed discovery. I regard the latter as the smaller scientific risk, although I admit that I cannot settle the B014 priority questions from the evidence in front of me. I would reconsider if the committee finds that firm-level selection is clearly a single, well-bounded achievement.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson moved from B050 to B009 after considering maturity and attribution. She keeps B050 as an alternative for a later year, because the neighbourhood-effect estimates are still being tested and the credit among Chetty, Hendren and Friedman is unsettled.
responses.response: I appreciate that you updated on the maturity and attribution points, and I think the move is well founded. It also removes one open question from the final discussion, because B050 is no longer a competing preferred part. I would add that I still regard B050 as a strong candidate in a later cycle, once cross-country replication is more complete. I agree with you on B009's own boundary: if the citation is narrowed to the trade-shock design, Dorn has a stronger claim than Katz. I would accept that substitution on that basis, and I would not call either trio clearly wrong.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will define the B009 achievement as the combined technology, trade and wage-structure account, which supports Katz, or as the China-shock evidence alone, which supports Dorn.
Whether Katz's work is distinct enough from Goldin's 2023 prize that its marginal credit is defensible, as I read it, or whether Dreber Almenberg's concern should weigh more.
The persistence, magnitude and external validity of the shift-share trade-shock estimates, which remain disputed in the literature.
Whether the technology and trade strands are one discovery or two. If the committee judges them to be two, I would move toward B014.

Whether the priority claims in B014 (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum, Hopenhayn) can be resolved by wording the citation around selection and reallocation, which I cannot settle from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for Autor, Katz or Hanson, and I note none for Dorn, whom I discuss as an excluded name. My documented connections are to Lund colleagues, co-authors in economic history, and the political scientist Johannes Lindvall, and none of them is credited on any shortlisted entry. My own work on electrification and labour outcomes is in an adjacent literature on technology and labour markets, but it is not a connection to a candidate. B040 remains adjacent to my work on railroads and the state, and I see no personal connection to its credited names. Katz is also credited in B050, and I do not propose crediting him twice. These are disclosed and not adjudicated, and I claim no independent verification.
